name: Treaty with the Winnebago, 1859
promises: Article 1: the eastern part of the Blue Earth reservation in Minnesota (townships 106 and 107, ranges 24 and 25, and two adjoining strips) "set apart and retained by them", with up to 80 acres for each head of a family and 40 acres for each single man, and the whole to be known as the Winnebago reservation.

Article 1: assigned tracts for the "exclusive use and benefit" of the holders and their heirs, not to be sold except to the United States or other members, and exempt from taxation, levy, sale or forfeiture until Congress provided otherwise.
Article 1: no white person except government employees allowed to live on or go onto the reservation without written permission.
Article 2: the western part of the reservation sold in parcels to the highest bidder, the proceeds used to build houses and provide tools and stock for the Ho-Chunk.
Article 3: the tribe's debts paid out of the sale proceeds.

breaches.what: Less than two years after this treaty took effect, Congress authorised the President to remove the Ho-Chunk from Minnesota and ordered the reservation they had kept under Article 1 appraised, opened to pre-emption and settlement and sold. The Act contains no provision for Ho-Chunk consent.

source.title: Act for the Removal of the Winnebago Indians, and for the Sale of their Reservation in Minnesota for their Benefit, 12 Stat. 658

breaches.quote: to effect the peaceful and quiet removal of the said Indians from the State of Minnesota

breaches.what: Before the Indian Claims Commission the Ho-Chunk claimed compensation for the part of the reservation sold under this treaty (Royce Area 416) and the part sold under the 1863 Act (Royce Area 439). The claims were settled within a $4,600,000 compromise of Dockets 243 to 245.

source.title: Winnebago Tribe and Nation v. United States, Dockets 243, 244 and 245, Findings of Fact on Compromise Settlement, September 3, 1970 (23 Ind. Cl. Comm. 467)
source.publisher: Oklahoma State University Libraries, Indian Claims Commission Decisions

landTaken: The 1863 Act directed that the whole remaining reservation be appraised and sold; the Act gives no acreage.
compensation: The 1863 Act directed that sale proceeds, after the debts secured by Article 3 of this treaty, be spent on improvements on a new reservation. In 1870 a compromise final judgment of $4,600,000 covered the Ho-Chunk claims in Dockets 243, 244 and 245, including Royce Areas 416 and 439.
today: In 1870 Congress directed the Secretary of the Interior to investigate the claims of Ho-Chunk still lawfully living in Minnesota and to issue patents for lands allotted to them under this treaty that had not been sold (Act of July 15, 1870, sec. 9, 16 Stat. 361). The Ho-Chunk Nation of Wisconsin and the Winnebago Tribe of Nebraska are the successors.

nationVoice.summary: The Tribe's history page says its people were moved from what is now northeast Iowa to Minnesota and then South Dakota before treaties of 1865 and 1874 set up its reservation in Nebraska.

openQuestions: The Act of February 21, 1863 is also recorded as its own queue entry (cession-1863-02-21-winnebago); the same breach appears in both files.
No government source opened here states that the Ho-Chunk took no part in the 1862 US-Dakota War, which was the setting of the 1863 Act.
The compromise does not allocate the $4,600,000 among the separate cessions.
No Ho-Chunk Nation account of this treaty or the removal was opened.

plain.promised: The Ho-Chunk kept the eastern part of their Blue Earth reservation in Minnesota, to be divided into family farms that could not be taxed or sold, while the western part was sold for their benefit.
plain.happened: In 1863 Congress ordered the Ho-Chunk removed from Minnesota and the land they had kept appraised, opened to settlers and sold. The Act made no provision for their consent.
plain.today: The Ho-Chunk claims for these lands were settled in a $4,600,000 Indian Claims Commission compromise in 1970 that also covered other cessions.
